subject: mixed effect model: ADVI and Maximum Likelihood results are very different

messages.author: c052ac5727650828
messages.subject: mixed effect model: ADVI and Maximum Likelihood results are very different
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I am trying to develop a mixed effect model using rstan. Given that beta_0 and beta (intercept and the coefficient of the fixed effect) are treated as parameters (improper prior), I expect the results to be very close to maximum likelihood estimation. I want to estimate $h^2$ which is basically the variance explained by the random effect. Using maximum likelihood estimation (more specifically Restricted maximum Likelihood estimation), I expect values around 0.5 for $h^2$ with standard error of around 0.07. Sure, SE is not the same as posterior of variance but at least the posterior mean should be close to ML.
I couldn’t get NUTS to run for this because; it stopped at the warm up step for about 8 hrs; perhaps due to the size of the problem. So I switched to ADVI. The results is very different than ML. Estimated $h2$ is around 0 and intercept does not look correct either. Any idea? Am I missing something?

(N is around 4500 and M is 8)

        mean   sd  10%   50%   90%
beta_0 11.21 1.13 9.74 11.23 12.71
h2      0.03 0.00 0.02  0.03  0.03

This is the code:

####### MODEL
mixed_model<-'
  data {
     int<lower=1> N;  // number of subjects
  int<lower=1> M;  // number of covariates
  vector[N]  y;       // height of subjects
  matrix[N,M]  X;  // covariates
  cov_matrix[N]   K; 
  }

  transformed data {
  cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;
  vector[N]  mu0 ;
  matrix[N,N] eye;

  L <- cholesky_decompose(K) ;

  for (j in 1:N) {
  mu0[j] <- 0;
  }

  for (j in 1:N) {
    for (i in 1:N) {
    eye[i,j] <- 0.0;
    }
      eye[j,j] <- 1.0;
    }
  }

  parameters {

  real beta_0;
  // coefficient of the fixed effect
  vector[M]  beta ;
  // Inverse of the Population standard deviation
  real<lower=0> sigma_inv;

  // proportion of variance (h2)
  real<lower=0,upper=1>  h2 ;

  vector[N]  g;

  // environment noise
  //vector[N]  epsilon;
  }

  transformed parameters  {
  // combination of the intercept and the fixed effect
  vector[N]  mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;  

  // Individual mean
  mu <- X * beta + beta_0 ;

  // get the Population standard deviation from its inverse
  sigma <- 1 / sigma_inv ;  

  }

  model {

  sigma_inv ~ gamma(0.001,0.001) ;
  h2 ~ uniform(0,1) ;

  // data generation
  g ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu0, sqrt(h2*sigma) * L) ;

  // noise generation
  //epsilon ~ normal( 0, (1 - h2)*sigma  ) ;

  // observation
  //y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu + g , sqrt( (1 - h2)*sigma )*eye ) ;
  for (j in 1:N) {
     y[j] ~ normal( mu[j] + g[j], (1-h2)*sigma ) ;
  }

  }
'

########## RUN the model
library(rstan)

model <- stan_model(model_code = mixed_model)
data <- list(N=N, M=M, y=c(y), K=K, X=X)
fit <- vb(model, data=data, algorithm='fullrank', iter=5000 )

        mean   sd  10%   50%   90%
beta_0 11.21 1.13 9.74 11.23 12.71
h2      0.03 0.00 0.02  0.03  0.03

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mixed effect model: ADVI and Maximum Likelihood results are very different
parts:
You don't have an intercept in that X matrix, do you? If
so, the model's not going to be identified and it can cause
serious slowdowns if not outright failures (see the manual chapter
on problematic posteriors). You might also want to add a prior
to beta --- in fact, it'll be necessary if there are strong
collinearities in the columns of X.

I don't know about your particular model, but the posterior mode
can be very far away from the posterior mean in general, and both can
be far away from the MLE. With improper priors,
you get infinite prior mass in the tails, so they're not no-ops in
the sense you might expect. In the asymptotic limit, with a fixed
prior, the posterior mean (and mode) will approach the MLE.

You can define a unit-diagonal (NxN) matrix as diag_matrix(rep_vector(1, N))
without the loops (that's just for convenience --- it won't be any faster).

This

> for (j in 1:N) {
> y[j] ~ normal( mu[j] + g[j], (1-h2)*sigma ) ;
> }

can be vectorized as

y ~ normal(mu + g, (1 - h2) * sigma);

You should just define sigma as a parameter, not sigma_inv, though
the implied improper priors will differ by a Jacobian (doesn't affect
the MLE, which isn't based on a full probabilty modle, but it does affect
the Bayesian posterior and poterior mode).

Also be careful that our multi-normal is based on co*variance* whereas
our univariate normal is parameterized by scale (std dev).

- Bob

Thank you Bob for your reply and sorry for my late reply (I was in a conference).

Thank you for your points, those were very helpful. My model here is a basic mixed effect model (see below), I believe that ML and posterior mean values should be close. For improper prior for beta, we expect MAP and ML to be the same. Plus the values have real meaning (here height of the individuals) and from experimental results and other independent studies study we know the approximate inferred heritability of height (h^2: heritability of height). Unfortunately ML and the posterior mean are orders of magnitudes different. While infrared ML for $h^2$ is > 0.5 (close to what we expect) the posterior mean is 0.015 using ADVI. I feel either I am missing something or ADVI is not working. Another sign is that y (height) is in centimeter, so the intercept (beta_1) should be > 100cm while the mean value on intercept is around 8cm . One more sign that ADVI is not working is that I have tried this model in pymc3 and if I wait long enough NUTS in pymc3 almost produces ML value (very slow). So far, I have not been able to get NUTS working in RStan. It stays in the in iteration 1 in the warm up stage for many hours without moving while CPU seems occupied.

An idea how to get this to work?

I modified the code (vectorized as you suggested) and looked into the data to make sure that the intercept is not added. Here is the updated code (any further improvement):

####### MODEL

     cov_matrix[N]   K; // GRM matrix
  }

  transformed data {
    cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;

    matrix[N,N] eye;

    L <- cholesky_decompose(K) ;

    for (j in 1:N) {
       mu0[j] <- 0;
    }
  }

  parameters {
  // Define parameters to estimate

  // coefficient of the fixed effect
  vector[M]  beta ;

  // variance of the Population standard deviation
  real<lower=0> sigma2 ;

  // heritability (h2)
  real<lower=0,upper=1>  h2 ;

  // random genetic effect
  vector[N]  g;

  }

  transformed parameters  {
  // combination of the intercept and the fixed effect
  vector[N]  mu;

  // Individual mean
  mu <- X * beta  ;

  }

  model {

  sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(0.001,0.001) ; 
  h2 ~ uniform(0,1) ;

  // data generation
  g ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu0, sqrt(h2*sigma2) * L) ;


  // observation
  y  ~ normal(mu + g, sqrt( (1 - h2) * sigma2 ) ); 

  }
'

########## RUN the model
library(rstan)

# to run ADVI
#rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
#options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
model <- stan_model(model_code = heritability_code)
data <- list(N=N, M=M, y=c(y), K=K, X=X)
fit <- vb(model, data=data, algorithm='fullrank', iter=5000 )
save(fit, file='/scratch/users/batmanghelich/fit.vb.RDATA')

parts:
Don't do this:
 sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(0.001,0.001) ; 

Instead, just put a prior on sigma directly, for example a half-normal or half-Cauchy with peak at 0.

A

parts:
Hi Andrew,

Thank you for your reply. I replaced inverse Gamma with half-Cauchy(0,5) and the results is not that different. NUTS has stayed in the warm-up stage for last 10hrs. Using ADVI, the posterior mean is orders of magnitude lower than maximum likelihood estimation (I expect the proportion of variance explained to be > 0.5 while it produces 0.01). The mean intercept is very low and posterior mean of variance is very high. I have attached the results, model, and the code below:


Any idea?


Results:

model:

code:

Don't do this:
 sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(0.001,0.001) ; 

Instead, just put a prior on sigma directly, for example a half-normal or half-Cauchy with peak at 0.

Thank you Bob for your reply and sorry for my late reply (I was in a conference).

Thank you for your points, those were very helpful. My model here is a basic mixed effect model (see below), I believe that ML and posterior mean values should be close. For improper prior for beta, we expect MAP and ML to be the same. Plus the values have real meaning (here height of the individuals) and from experimental results and other independent studies study we know the approximate inferred heritability of height (h^2: heritability of height). One more sign that ADVI is not working is that I have tried this model in pymc3 and if I wait long enough NUTS in pymc3 almost produces ML value (very slow). On Tuesday, 7 June 2016 15:25:58 UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:



You don't have an intercept in that X matrix, do you?  If
so, the model's not going to be identified and it can cause
serious slowdowns if not outright failures (see the manual chapter
on problematic posteriors).  You might also want to add a prior
to beta --- in fact, it'll be necessary if there are strong
collinearities in the columns of X.

I don't know about your particular model, but the posterior mode
can be very far away from the posterior mean in general, and both can
be far away from the MLE.  With improper priors,
you get infinite prior mass in the tails, so they're not no-ops in
the sense you might expect.  In the asymptotic limit, with a fixed
prior, the posterior mean (and mode) will approach the MLE.

You can define a unit-diagonal (NxN) matrix as diag_matrix(rep_vector(1, N))
without the loops (that's just for convenience --- it won't be any faster).

This

> for (j in 1:N) {
>      y[j] ~ normal( mu[j] + g[j], (1-h2)*sigma ) ;
>   }

can be vectorized as

  y ~ normal(mu + g, (1 - h2) * sigma);

You should just define sigma as a parameter, not sigma_inv, though
the implied improper priors will differ by a Jacobian (doesn't affect
the MLE, which isn't based on a full probabilty modle, but it does affect
the Bayesian posterior and poterior mode).

Also be careful that our multi-normal is based on co*variance* whereas
our univariate normal is parameterized by scale (std dev).

- Bob
